tracks.title: Provenance that travels with the bytes
tracks.text: Lesson one point three — signatures. This one is a sub-lesson, under workbook… the parent lesson, where the file is the unit. Provenance that travels with the bytes. [curious] A signature, here, is an embedded manifest — an Ed25519 manifest, signed by a self-certifying did key, and read by two independent checks. Who signed… and whether the bytes changed. No certificate authority. No registry. No network. The proof rides inside the file it attests… and verifying it needs nothing but the file. This lesson is how that trick actually works — and where it honestly stops.

tracks.title: Forwarded twice, edited once
tracks.text: Forwarded twice… edited once. [sighs] The whole workbook pitch is one sentence — hand the file to anyone. And the moment you do, you lose the one thing every platform hands you for free. Knowing where the bytes came from… and whether anyone touched them on the way. A workbook forwarded through three inboxes looks exactly like one that was quietly edited in the second inbox. There is no tell. The bytes don't remember. Now picture that journey. An author signs a workbook. It lands in inbox one… which forwards it. It lands in inbox two… which edits one line, quietly. It lands in inbox three… which forwards it on. And at the end stands a question with no answer — which copy is real? The edit in the middle is invisible to everyone downstream. And here's the cruel part — every reflex fix breaks the format that made the pitch worth making. A detached signature file is a second file… and one file was the entire point. A registry lookup needs a server… and the file is supposed to work offline, in ten years, on a thumb drive. Platform-checked provenance needs the platform… and the file just left it. So the requirement is awkward and specific. The proof has to ride inside the artifact, survive being copied byte for byte, and be checkable by anyone holding the file alone.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A signature is an embedded Ed25519 manifest — carried under a workbooks content type — signed by a self-certifying did key, and verified by two checks. Who signed… and whether the bytes changed. Valid means both. [curious] It borrows C2PA's vocabulary — manifests, assertions, actions — and drops C2PA's machinery on purpose. No COSE envelope. No X five oh nine chain. No external tool. Just Ed25519 over canonical JSON, with the signer's identity expressed as a did key. Now let me read you the real thing — the signed block, lifted from a freshly signed file. It's a script tag that sits just before the closing body tag. Inside it, a small JSON object with seven fields, sorted alphabetically. First… assertions — what's being claimed, here c2pa action published, meaning this was shipped. Second… asset s h a two fifty-six — the fingerprint of the page without this block. Third… claim generator — the name of the signing tool, w b cli for the command line, workbooks runtime for the engine. A breadcrumb for which tool signed. Fourth… issued at — a U T C claim of when. Fifth… issuer did — the signer's identity. Sixth… signature — the Ed25519 bytes, in base sixty-four. And last… version — v one. Seven fields. And that alphabetical order is not cosmetic. It's load-bearing — and two sections from now you'll see exactly why.

tracks.title: Why verify asks two questions
tracks.text: Why does verify ask two questions? Because one boolean could never tell you what you need to know. Verifying returns a small record, and the field that matters is the last one — valid equals signature AND asset integrity. Two checks, ANDed together. [curious] Picture the fork. Verify runs, and it splits into two paths that never touch. The first path is the signature check — Ed25519 over the manifest, using a public key decoded from the did key itself. The second path is the asset integrity check — s h a two fifty-six of the page, with every manifest block stripped out first. Both come back true… and only then do they meet at an AND gate that lights up valid, true. If either one comes back false… valid is false. Now think through the four ways those two checks can land. First case — signature true, integrity true. Signed by this key, bytes untouched. Valid. Second case — and this is the one to hold in your head — signature true, integrity false. That means the file was edited after signing. The manifest itself is intact… but the page around it is not. Invalid. Third case — signature false, integrity true. The manifest itself was tampered with, or the key doesn't match. Invalid. And the fourth — no manifest at all. That's not invalid… it's an error, plainly, nothing was ever signed. [excited] Sit with that second case. Edit a single character in the body of a signed workbook, and the signature check stays true — the manifest block is exactly as it was signed — while integrity flips false, because the bytes around it moved. One construct telling you the seal is genuine… but the envelope was opened. A single yes-or-no could never say both of those at once.

tracks.title: Signing a file from inside it
tracks.text: Signing a file from inside it. [curious] There's a chicken-and-egg buried in that phrase — the signature rides inside the file. To sign the bytes, you need to hash them. But the moment you inject the signature, you've changed the bytes you just hashed. Hash again, and you'd need to re-sign. Re-sign, and the bytes change again. The snake eats its tail. One trick dissolves it… strip, then hash. Hash the file as if no manifest were there. Remove every manifest block first, take the s h a two fifty-six of what remains, and store that. Now injecting the manifest can't invalidate the hash — because the hash was always computed over the manifest-free page. And verification re-strips and re-hashes exactly the same way, so the numbers line up. Let me walk you the whole sign path, step by step. First… strip any prior manifest blocks from the file. Second… take s h a two fifty-six of that stripped page, and that becomes the asset fingerprint. Third… fill in the rest of the manifest — version, issuer, claim generator, the timestamp, the assertions. Fourth… serialize it the canonical way — sorted, compact. Fifth… Ed25519-sign those bytes, and base sixty-four the result into the signature field. And sixth… inject the finished block as a script tag, just before the closing body tag. [excited] Two details earn their keep. The block goes just before the closing body — or gets appended if there isn't one. And signing is idempotent — it strips all prior manifest blocks before writing the new one. So re-signing replaces, never stacks. Sign a file ten times… and it carries exactly one signature. The last. That's what lets check-in re-sign on every single save without piling up dead seals.

tracks.title: The name that is the key
tracks.text: The name that is the key. This is a depth rung — skippable — but it's the idea that let the entire C2PA stack get deleted. [curious] A did key is an identity that IS its own public key. There's nothing to look up. The verifier doesn't fetch a certificate or query a registry to learn whose key signed — it reads the key straight out of the identifier string. The construction is exact, and you can picture the layout as four segments laid end to end. First segment… the literal text, did colon key colon — the method, a key expressed inline. Second… a single letter z — the multibase tag saying base fifty-eight follows. Third… two bytes, E D zero one — the multicodec that means this is an Ed25519 key. And fourth… the thirty-two bytes of the actual public key itself. Prefix, codec, key — encoded together into one string. Here's the lovely consequence. Because every Ed25519 did key begins with that same E D zero one prefix, every single one of them encodes to a string starting did key z six M k. That prefix is a tell you can read by eye. And the decode side is strict — anything that isn't thirty-four bytes, or doesn't start with E D zero one, gets rejected as not an Ed25519 did key. Same form Radicle uses, same form the W three C spec defines. Interoperable… not bespoke. [excited] Self-certifying is the property that pays for everything else. Because the key is the name, the signature check needs nothing but the string in front of it. It collapses two questions a certificate scheme keeps separate — is this signature valid, and does this identity own that key — into one operation. Because the identity and the key are the same bytes. No certificate hierarchy survives that collapse… which is exactly why the X five oh nine spike got marked superseded and shelved.

tracks.title: The one byte contract
tracks.text: The one byte contract. Another depth rung. [curious] A signature is over bytes — not over some idea of the manifest. So two programs that want to make and check each other's signatures must serialize the same manifest to the same bytes, every time. Or a signature minted by one fails in the other. That shared serialization is canonical JSON. The rules are short — recursively sort every object's keys by string order, emit compact with no whitespace, U T F eight, scalars JSON-encoded. Now compare the same manifest two ways. Pretty-printed, it has the author's key order and is indented and spaced — and it hashes to one number, and that number does not verify. Canonical, the keys are sorted, the whitespace is gone — it hashes to a different number, and that number is the one that was signed. Only the canonical form verifies. And this is why the signed block earlier had its fields alphabetized — assertions, asset hash, claim generator, issued at, issuer did, signature, version. That's the canonical sort, written out. The Elixir version and the Rust version are the same fifteen lines, twice — and the Rust file header says it out loud, byte-compatible with the Elixir manifest. That comment is the contract, written down. [curious] If the two ever drifted by a single space, a command-line-signed workbook would fail runtime verify… and the whole cross-tool promise would quietly break.

tracks.title: Where the private half lives
tracks.text: Where the private half lives. A depth rung on the keys themselves. Every signature needs a private key, and there are two keystores in play. They share an on-disk format… but they hold independent keys. Which means the command-line tool signs as a different identity than the runtime tenant — true by construction, not by accident. Let me lay the two side by side. The command-line key lives in the app directory, a hex seed plus a public file, minted on your first sign from the operating system's randomness, with the private half locked down to owner-only permissions. The runtime tenant key lives in a dot-workbooks folder inside the tenant's repo, same hex-seed format, minted per tenant by the Erlang crypto library, and gitignored — never committed. [sighs] The runtime side has a durability problem worth stating plainly. A container's filesystem is wiped on redeploy. Without persistence, every redeploy would mint a fresh key… hence a fresh did… breaking every signature that tenant ever made. The fix is one secret — the primary tenant's seed is restored deterministically from an environment variable, base sixty-four of the thirty-two-byte seed, held as a Fly secret, with the primary tenant chosen by a second variable that defaults to dev. Set it, and the primary tenant's did survives redeploys. Don't… and it doesn't. [curious] And here's the unifying idea — one key, many rails. The same per-tenant Ed25519 key signs three things. First, artifacts — the manifest on a workbook. Second, the agent run ledger — a hash-chain head, sealed by the same key. And third, toolkit manifests — author did and signature lines in the toolkit file. One identity key… no second store to keep in sync. That's a deliberate anti-drift stance — and it's why the same did shows up all across the system.

tracks.title: Where signing fires for you
tracks.text: Where signing fires for you. You can always sign by hand — sign on the command line, sign on the runtime, both fully local, no engine required. But signing also fires automatically, at the moments where provenance matters most. Picture the artifact's lifecycle with three checkpoints marked on it. [curious] First checkpoint… ship on egress. When a bundle ships with a tenant in context, it signs the workbook with the tenant did, records signed equals true in the bundle's manifest, and stamps the assertion c2pa action published. That's the moment the file leaves home. Second checkpoint… library check-in. Every check-in re-signs the workbook, this time with the assertion c2pa action updated — so the provenance tracks each revision. And third checkpoint… the third-party install gate. A toolkit-workbook install can demand a signature — set require signature to true, and then the bundle verify must come back valid, or the install simply fails, refused as a bad signature. That gate is off by default for first-party local installs — it's the posture you reach for when you're installing something you didn't make. [excited] And toolkit manifests get the same crypto in a different envelope — signing the manifest body with signature and author did lines, required for third-party trust. Meanwhile, pure-local bundle assembly writes signed equals false — because there, signing is a separate, explicit step. Never a silent default.

tracks.title: What it is not
tracks.text: Now the honest part — what it is not. And this one has teeth, because a self-signed signature is easy to over-read. [sighs] The hard truth — this proves continuity, not identity. Verify tells you the bytes are untampered since they were signed, by the holder of this key. It does not tell you who that holder is. There is no trust list. No revocation. No expiry. Self-certifying means self-asserted — and the design doc says it directly. Self-signed is provenance only. Trust-listing is a distribution concern for later. The sharpest consequence — anyone can strip the manifest and re-sign with their own key. The scheme detects tampering under a claimed identity… it does not prevent re-attribution. Strip and re-sign always succeeds, and the result verifies cleanly under the new signer's did. The only defense is out of band — you compare the issuer did against one you already trust. And let me be exact about today's gap. The install gate checks only that the signature is valid. It does not compare against an allowlisted did. So the gate currently proves validly signed by someone… not signed by an author I chose. An honest gap, named. Three smaller limits round it out. First — the issued-at timestamp is a claim, not a proof. There's no timestamping authority, so the field is just the signer's word for when. Second — it won't show a Content Credentials badge in C2PA-aware tools, because the content type isn't a real C2PA claim. A real badge would need the X five oh nine chain that got shelved. And third — multi-tenant durability is unfinished. Only the primary tenant's did survives a redeploy. Others re-mint, until bring-your-own-storage lands. [curious] What you get, stated without inflation — untampered since signed, by the holder of this key. That's real, and useful. It is not trusted… and this lesson won't pretend the two are the same.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Is this real C2PA? No — and that's deliberate. It borrows the vocabulary and drops the machinery. No COSE, no X five oh nine, no external tool. Pure Ed25519 over canonical JSON with a did key issuer. What happens if I edit a signed workbook? Verify fails on integrity — signature stays true, integrity flips false, valid is false. To re-attest the new bytes, re-sign — and because signing is idempotent, the new signature replaces the old one. Can someone re-sign my workbook as theirs? [chuckles] Yes — and it verifies cleanly under their did. But it's signed as them, not as you, and a verifier who knows your did sees a stranger. The scheme proves tamper-evidence under a claimed identity — it doesn't stop re-attribution. Do I need the runtime to verify? No. Verify on the command line is fully local — it decodes the public key out of the did, strips the manifest, re-hashes, and checks the signature. No network, no account. Does the signature survive bundling? Yes — the manifest lives in the workbook file, which sits inside the bundle, and bundle verify runs the same two checks over it. And — can I sign on one machine and verify on another? Yes. The did carries the public key, so the verifying machine needs nothing from the signer but the file itself.

tracks.title: Back up to the workbook
tracks.text: So that's signatures. An embedded manifest, a self-certifying name, and two checks that answer two different questions — who signed, and whether the bytes changed. The whole thing proves continuity, honestly… not identity. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under workbook — lesson one — the file that is the unit, the one whose seal we just spent twelve minutes unpacking. From there, two neighbors sit close. Bundles… for the egress moment where signing fires. And w b x… for sign and verify as local verbs you can run right now. The seal travels with the file. Now you know how to read it.
